did_you_know.text: The words “statutes” and “judgments” are not identical: statutes are binding commands, while judgments are more closely connected with law and justice between people.
In the ancient Near East, hilltops, high places, and leafy trees were common sites of worship. The verse therefore mentions several kinds of natural settings associated with idolatry.
The “Asherim” were usually wooden cult objects associated with the worship of the goddess Asherah. The term shows that this worship involved physical symbols, not only statues.
Notice that Deuteronomy 12 speaks of “the place the Lord will choose” but does not name Jerusalem here. The identification of that place with Jerusalem appears later in the biblical story.
The worship described here includes a joyful meal with the whole household. Even servants, who usually had little social status, are included in the religious celebration.
The tribe of Levi did not receive one continuous territorial inheritance like the other tribes. Levites therefore lived in different towns and depended on support from the surrounding community.
Gazelles and deer were familiar wild animals in ancient Israel. Comparing ordinary meat-eating to eating them emphasizes that not every meal of meat had to be part of a sacrifice.
In the Torah, blood is associated with life, so it may not be eaten. Pouring it onto the ground expresses respect for life and for the act of eating.
When the land expands and the distance from the religious center becomes greater, the Torah allows meat to be eaten in local settlements. This shows attention to geographical realities.
For ordinary meat—that is, meat that is not a sacrifice—a ritually impure person and a pure person may eat together. This differs from the stricter rules governing sacred food.
